overview: Linked List topic me 3 bade skills hain: (1) node-manipulation code trace karna (pointers reassign ho rahe hain, resulting list kya banegi), (2) insertion/deletion ki complexity samajhna (pointer-given vs search-needed cases), (3) linked-list vs array trade-offs jaanna.
whyItMatters: 24 PYQs, aur Trees/Graphs jaisी advanced structures isi 'node + pointer' mental model par based hain.
coreConcept: Linked List = nodes ki chain, har node me DATA + NEXT pointer (agle node ka address). Array se bada difference: CONTIGUOUS memory nahi chahiye, aur INSERTION/DELETION O(1) hai AGAR pointer already mil chuka hai (position dhoondhna O(n) hai, but ek baar mil gaya to modify O(1)).
hinglishExplanation: Linked list ko ek 'treasure hunt chain' socho — har clue (node) tumhe agle clue ka address deta hai, khud pura map nahi. Isliye BEECH me kahin insert/delete karna sirf 2-3 pointers change karke ho jaata hai (fast), LEKIN us jagah tak PAHUNCHNE ke liye tumhe chain follow karni padti hai shuru se (slow, O(n)) — array me jaise directly index[5] pe kood sakte the, yahan nahi kood sakte.
formalDefinition: A linked list node contains data and a pointer to the next node. Singly linked: one 'next' pointer. Doubly linked: 'next' AND 'prev' pointers. Circular: last node points back to first.
importantProperties: Insert/Delete GIVEN a pointer to the target position: O(1) for the pointer-manipulation itself, but O(n) to delete a node in a SINGLY linked list if you're only given a pointer to the node itself (not its predecessor) — need the predecessor to update its 'next' (the classic exception: you CAN fake O(1) deletion by copying the next node's data into the current node and deleting the next node instead — works unless it's the LAST node).

In a DOUBLY linked list, deletion given just the node's own pointer IS truly O(1) (use prev pointer directly, no predecessor search needed) — this is the single biggest singly-vs-doubly trade-off tested.
Searching/finding a position by VALUE is always O(n) for any linked list (no random access) — this is why 'binary search on a linked list' doesn't give the usual O(log n) speedup.
Concatenating two lists in O(1) needs a pointer to the TAIL of the first list (or use a circular doubly linked list where the tail is always reachable in O(1) from the head).

formulas.searchWorstCase: O(n) — no random access, must traverse from head
formulas.insertDeleteWithPointer: O(1) once you HAVE the correct pointer(s); O(n) to find that pointer by value in a singly linked list
formulas.concatenationTime: O(1) with a tail pointer or circular list; O(n) without one (must traverse to find the end)

keyPropertiesAndIdentities: 'Delete node given ONLY a pointer to it' (not the head, not the predecessor) in a SINGLY linked list: fake it in O(1) by copying next node's data into this node and deleting the next node — FAILS if the given node is the LAST node (no next node to copy from), in which case true O(n) traversal from head is needed.
Binary search NEEDS random access (jump to the middle) — a linked list can't do this in O(1), so 'binary search on a linked list' is NOT efficient, despite the sorted order.
commonPitfalls: Assuming deletion given a node pointer is always O(1) in a SINGLY linked list — it's the special copy-and-delete-next trick, and it fails for the last node.
Confusing 'insertion is O(1)' (true, once you have the position) with 'inserting a value in sorted order is O(1)' (false — finding the right position is O(n)).
Assuming linked lists support efficient binary search (they don't — no random access).
standardTechniques: For code-tracing questions: draw the actual node boxes with arrows, and update the arrows step by step as each pointer-reassignment statement executes — never trust mental tracking for 3+ pointer reassignments.

For complexity questions: separate 'the pointer manipulation itself' (always O(1)) from 'finding the right pointer/position' (O(n) unless already given) — this distinction resolves most trick questions.

For singly vs doubly vs circular comparison questions: identify exactly which operation is being asked about and recall the specific trade-off for THAT operation (don't generalize 'doubly is always better').
